stories.headline: Update: Xi Hosts Putin Days After Trump, Projecting China as Global Power Broker
stories.summary:
Chinese President Xi Jinping received Russian President Vladimir Putin in Beijing on Wednesday with full state honors — a near-mirror of the ceremony afforded to U.S. President Donald Trump just days earlier. The back-to-back summits are a deliberate signal from Beijing that China positions itself as a central diplomatic player talking to all sides of global conflicts without binding itself to any single alliance.

Talks between Xi and Putin concluded with more than 20 agreements on trade and technology, but yielded no major breakthroughs and notably no approval for the stalled Siberian gas pipeline Russia has sought for years — underscoring the increasingly unequal nature of the partnership. Russia, isolated by Western sanctions and dependent on China as its largest trading partner and top buyer of oil and gas, arrived in a position of clear supplicant. Analysts noted that China has leverage over both Washington and Moscow given its dominance in rare earth minerals and advanced manufacturing.

The diplomatic choreography reflects a significant shift in global order. Five years ago China faced potential isolation; today it hosts the leaders of the world's two most consequential rival powers within the same week. Xi faces both Trump and Putin as leaders embroiled in costly, prolonged conflicts — Trump in the Middle East and Putin in Ukraine — giving Beijing unusual room to set terms of engagement.

No substantive peace initiatives emerged from either summit, and Western governments are watching closely to assess whether China will use its leverage to press Russia toward any settlement in Ukraine or whether the joint statement's vague language on multilateralism simply reinforces a China-Russia axis that challenges the post-Cold War international order.

stories.headline: Lithuania Leaders Take Shelter as Drone Alert Halts Vilnius; NATO Jets Scrambled
stories.summary:
Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda and Prime Minister Inga Ruginiene were evacuated to emergency shelters Wednesday after a drone alert brought the capital Vilnius to a standstill. Flights were suspended and road and rail traffic halted briefly; parliament was also evacuated, with politicians and staff moved to a basement shelter. The alert was later lifted without confirmed drone intercept.

Lithuania's national crisis management centre said the alert was triggered by a drone detected in neighboring Belarus that appeared to be heading toward Lithuanian territory. NATO jets were scrambled to locate and potentially intercept the drone but were unable to find it. The drone's origin and purpose had not been confirmed as of Wednesday evening.

The incident is the latest in a pattern of drone incursions over the three Baltic NATO member states — Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania — that has escalated sharply in recent weeks. A NATO jet shot down a suspected Ukrainian drone over Estonia on Tuesday. Latvia's prime minister resigned last week amid a political crisis over Russia-redirected Ukrainian drones straying into Latvian airspace, and two Ukrainian drones struck an empty Latvian oil storage site earlier this month.

Ukraine has blamed Russian electronic jamming for redirecting its drones aimed at military targets inside Russia, and has apologized to the Baltic states for unintended incursions. Russia has accused the Baltic nations of allowing Ukraine to use their airspace as corridors to strike Russian territory — a charge all three governments deny. The Kremlin said Wednesday it is monitoring the incidents closely and formulating a response.

stories.headline: Barney Frank, Architect of Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reforms and Gay Rights Trailblazer, Dies at 86
stories.summary:
Former U.S. Representative Barney Frank (D-Mass.) died Tuesday night at age 86, according to his former campaign manager and family. Frank served three decades in the House of Representatives and became one of the most prominent liberal lawmakers of his era, known for a sharp wit and combative floor style.

Frank's most enduring legislative achievement was the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act, enacted in 2010 in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis. The sweeping law overhauled financial regulation, created the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, and imposed new restrictions on large banks and derivatives markets. Republicans have long argued the law stifled lending and economic growth; supporters credited it with strengthening systemic safeguards against another financial collapse.

Frank also made history as one of the first openly gay members of Congress, coming out publicly in 1987 at a time when such a declaration carried significant political risk. He became a leading voice on LGBTQ rights throughout his tenure, which ended with his retirement in 2013. His career spanned the AIDS crisis, the repeal of 'Don't Ask, Don't Tell,' and the early legislative battles over same-sex marriage.

stories.headline: Update: Primary Results: Georgia Senate and Governor Races Head to Runoffs; Pennsylvania Dem Picks Union Leader
stories.summary:
Voters across multiple states cast ballots Tuesday in primary contests testing the shape of both parties heading into the 2026 midterms. In Georgia's Republican Senate primary, former University of Tennessee football coach Derek Dooley — backed heavily by Gov. Brian Kemp — advanced to a June 16 runoff against incumbent Rep. Mike Collins, while former Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger fell short in the Republican governor's primary, sending Lt. Gov. Burt Jones and billionaire Rick Jackson to a runoff.

On the Democratic side, former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms emerged as the Democratic nominee for Georgia governor, telling supporters she was "a fighter" ready for the general election campaign. In Pennsylvania, union leader and former firefighter Bob Brooks won the Democratic primary in a competitive congressional race, drawing endorsements from Sen. Bernie Sanders and Gov. Josh Shapiro.

The results carry national implications as both parties assess their positioning ahead of November. In Georgia, Gov. Kemp's ability to steer Dooley into a runoff signals ongoing tensions within the Republican Party between Trump-aligned and establishment factions. Raffensperger, who gained national prominence for resisting Trump's 2020 election pressure, said spending by better-funded rivals drowned out his message.

The Associated Press called races across the board as results came in Tuesday night. The Georgia runoffs are set for June 16, with both the Senate and governor contests still unresolved on the Republican side.

stories.headline: Update: WHO Reports 600 Suspected Ebola Cases, 139 Deaths as Outbreak Spreads Beyond DR Congo
stories.summary:
The World Health Organization reported Wednesday that the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has now reached 600 suspected cases and 139 suspected deaths, with confirmed cases also recorded in Uganda's capital Kampala. WHO Director-General Dr. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said the outbreak of the Bundibugyo species likely began "a couple of months ago" and that case counts are expected to rise further given delays in detection.

The outbreak is centered in DR Congo's eastern Ituri province, with additional cases in North Kivu — including rebel-controlled Goma. The two confirmed cases in Uganda both involved individuals who had traveled from DR Congo. The WHO declared a public health emergency of international concern on Sunday but said the situation does not yet rise to pandemic level, assessing global risk as low.

The Bundibugyo species presents particular challenges: it has not been seen in over a decade, there is no approved vaccine for it, and no targeted drug treatments exist. A vaccine used against the more common Zaire species may offer partial protection, but experimental options remain limited. The region's years of armed conflict further complicate containment efforts.

This is DR Congo's 17th Ebola outbreak. Health officials are working to trace contacts and establish treatment infrastructure in the affected gold-mining communities of Mongwalu and surrounding areas, where access is difficult.

stories.headline: NAACP Launches Boycott of Southern College Athletic Programs Over Voting Rights Rollback
stories.summary:
The NAACP announced Tuesday a campaign called "Out of Bounds" urging Black athletes, fans, and alumni to boycott the athletic programs of public universities in seven Southern states — Alabama, Florida, Georgia, Louisiana, Mississippi, Texas, and South Carolina — over what the civil rights organization describes as efforts to restrict Black voting representation. The campaign calls on prospective recruits, enrolled athletes, and donors to "withhold athletic and financial support" from flagship university programs.

The boycott is a direct response to redistricting actions by Republican state legislatures following a recent U.S. Supreme Court ruling that weakened a key provision of the Voting Rights Act of 1965. Activists argue that GOP-led states have used the ruling to eliminate majority-Black congressional districts, and the NAACP is targeting college athletics — an arena where Black talent disproportionately drives revenue — as a pressure point.

"Black athletes should not be asked to generate wealth, prestige, and power for state institutions while those same states strip political power from Black communities," said NAACP President Derrick Johnson. Supporters of the redistricting plans argue the maps comply with the Supreme Court's ruling and reflect legitimate political and geographic considerations. Republican state officials have defended the new district lines as lawful.

The near-term practical impact of the boycott may be limited: college football and basketball transfer portals are closed until 2027, and binding recruiting commitments have already been made for the upcoming season. However, advocates say the campaign could influence high school recruits weighing their choices for 2027 and beyond, potentially affecting programs that generate hundreds of millions of dollars annually.

stories.headline: Ukraine Strikes Russia's Norsi Oil Refinery for Second Time This Week
stories.summary:
Ukraine said Tuesday it struck Russia's major Norsi oil refinery in the Nizhny Novgorod region for the second time in a single week, continuing its campaign to degrade Russian energy infrastructure deep inside Russian territory. The refinery is one of Russia's largest and most strategically significant petroleum processing facilities.

The repeated strikes signal a Ukrainian effort to impose sustained economic and logistical costs on Moscow as ground fighting continues in the east. Some analysts have interpreted President Putin's recent statements about a potential truce as a stalling tactic rather than a genuine peace overture, noting that Russian forces have faced pressure along portions of the front line.

The attacks on energy infrastructure have been a central element of Ukraine's long-range strategy, aimed at reducing Russia's ability to fund and supply its war effort. Russia has responded with its own strikes on Ukrainian power and industrial infrastructure throughout the conflict.

The Norsi strikes come amid broader diplomatic activity, including ongoing U.S.-mediated discussions about a possible ceasefire framework, though no agreement has been reached. Ukraine has maintained that continued military pressure is essential leverage in any negotiations.
